name: Narrative bias
statement: Narrative bias is the finding that a few single-case stories shift risk judgements away from the statistical base rate shown alongside them.
meaning: Betsch, Haase, Renkewitz and Schmid define the target as 'the excessive influence of narrative information, exemplars, and testimonies, which we refer to as narrative bias'. The paradigm behind that sentence is fixed and narrow. A participant reads a statistic giving the rate of some adverse event, then reads a set of first-person reports of which a known share describe that event happening. If judgement tracked the statistic, the share would not matter. It does. Raising the share of reports describing the adverse event raises perceived risk and lowers stated willingness to accept the treatment. The claim is about how two samples of evidence get weighted, not about stories in general. Betsch and colleagues name Borgida and Nisbett's 1977 study as the classic case, in which brief personal accounts moved students' course choices more than mean course evaluations; that paper was not read for this entry. The same words carry two other meanings. Nassim Taleb's narrative fallacy, from chapter 6 of The Black Swan, is defined in his glossary as 'our need to fit a story or pattern to a series of connected or disconnected facts'. That is a claim about explanation, not about weighting evidence. Moore and colleagues use narrative bias for reporting spin. They define it as 'a tendency to interpret information as part of a larger story or pattern, regardless of whether the facts support the full narrative', and score it in the titles and abstracts of trials. Only the first of the three has been tested as a claim about people.

origin.who: Cornelia Betsch, Corina Ulshöfer, Frank Renkewitz and Tilmann Betsch
origin.note: The experiments that fixed the paradigm. Their abstract reports two studies in a simulated online bulletin board, the second crossing statistical risk of 20% or 40% against 2 or 4 of 10 narratives reporting adverse events, and finds a stronger influence of the number of narratives than of the statistic. The label narrative bias is not in that abstract. It appears in the group's later papers, and the 2015 follow-up is the one that states it as a definition. Taleb's narrative fallacy is nine years older as a phrase and is a different claim, described above. The earliest use of narrative bias in the present sense located here is the 2013 paper by Betsch, Renkewitz and Haase; no source claiming to coin either phrase was found.

evidence: The follow-up that carries the name was read in full. Betsch, Haase, Renkewitz and Schmid ran two experiments. Experiment 1 used 277 students at the University of Erfurt, mean age 22.16. The design was 2 × 2 × 3 between subjects. It crossed the statistical rate of vaccine adverse events, 5% or 40%, against the share of 20 first-person reports describing an adverse event, also 5% or 40%. Which of three measures came first was the third factor. The statistic appeared as a percentage and as a 100-square pictograph. On a visual analog risk scale, answered first by 94 subjects, the reports outweighed the statistic: standardised β = .43, p < .001 for the reports against β = .29, p = .002 for the base rate. On a percent probability estimate, answered first by 89 subjects, the ranking reversed, β = .81, p < .001 for the statistic against β = .15, p = .02 for the reports. The authors also report a negativity bias on the risk scale, where the reports raised perceived risk more than they lowered it, while the percent estimates moved symmetrically. Experiment 2 recruited 464 people through Amazon Mechanical Turk for US$1, held the statistic at 20%, and set the share of adverse-event reports at 10%, 20% or 40%. Perceived risk again tracked the reports, β = .38, p < .001, n = 168. Doubling the pool of reports from 10 to 20 while holding the share constant changed nothing, and reading times show subjects spent twice as long on 20 reports as on 10. Three checks on the procedure left the effect standing. It was as strong when reading the reports was optional as when it was required, F(1,92) = 19.11, p < .001, ηp² = .17, and 78.2% of those offered the choice read them. It was unchanged when the statistic came after the reports instead of before, F(1,109) = 16.07, p < .001, ηp² = .13. Numerate subjects showed a weaker bias than innumerate ones. Four other papers from the same group were read only as abstracts. Betsch, Ulshöfer, Renkewitz and Betsch report that the number of narratives influenced judgement more than the statistical risk did, and that emotional narratives moved perceived risk more than unemotional ones while richness had no effect. Betsch, Renkewitz and Haase ran 458 participants through a simulated patient network. They report that summary statistics had the smallest impact, narratives more, and both together the most, and that a disclaimer warning of the bias reduced the influence of the network. Haase, Betsch and Renkewitz gave 265 people reports attributed either to an anti-vaccination website or to a neutral health forum. They report a stable narrative bias unaffected by credibility cues, with the anti-vaccination attribution lowering perceived risk overall. Haase, Schmid and Betsch ran three online experiments with 564 subjects, varying the share of adverse-event reports at 5%, 20% and 35% against a 20% statistic. Risk perceptions and intentions moved in both directions. Neither likelihood of infection, severity of disease nor perceived susceptibility changed the size of the shift. Independent groups get less tidy results. Ubel, Jepson and Baron gave prospective jurors in Philadelphia County statistics on angioplasty and bypass surgery together with patient testimonials. In their first study 44% chose bypass when the mix of testimonials matched the statistics and 30% when it did not, P = 0.002. In their second study the same contrast gave 37% against 34%, P = 0.59, and 58% of a group shown no testimonials at all chose bypass. Fagerlin, Wang and Ubel used the same scenario. The anecdotes moved choices when the statistics were in prose, 41% against 20% choosing bypass, χ² = 14.40, P < 0.001. They did not when the statistics were reinforced with a pictograph and a quiz, 38% against 44%, χ² = 1.08, P > 0.20. Their second study concludes that the quiz alone did not reduce the influence of the anecdotes and the pictograph did. Obrecht, Chapman and Gelman report higher estimates of event frequency when individual cases arrived one at a time than when the same cases were summarised. Subjects treated each data sample as a single instance rather than weighting it by its size. A wider question, which is not this one, is whether narrative messages persuade better than statistical ones. Freling, Yang, Saini, Itani and Abualsamh meta-analysed 61 papers yielding 160 observations and 32,321 participants, and report a mean Hedges's g of 0.066, 95% bootstrapped interval 0.039 to 0.093, in favour of statistical evidence. Threat severity, personal relevance and health content each reversed the sign, at g = -0.12, g = -0.16 and g = -0.11 respectively. That meta-analysis excluded Betsch and colleagues' 2011 paper for combining the two kinds of evidence in one message, which is the design the narrative bias is measured in.

replication.headline: The effect holds across the Erfurt group's experiments and appears in independent work. It disappears when the statistic is drawn as a pictograph, when the judgement is asked for as a percentage, and in one of two studies by an independent team.
replication.detail: Betsch, Haase, Renkewitz and Schmid tested the effect against six competing explanations and it survived all of them. It did not depend on the absolute number of reports, on whether they were read by choice or by instruction, or on their position relative to the statistic. Source credibility, disease risk and a statistic already shown as a pictograph left it standing too. What it did depend on is the question asked. The same 277 subjects gave β = .43 for the reports on a visual analog risk scale and β = .15 on a percent probability estimate, where the base rate took β = .81. Independent teams split. Ubel, Jepson and Baron found testimonials moving treatment choice by 14 percentage points in one study, P = 0.002, and by 3 points in the next, P = 0.59. Fagerlin, Wang and Ubel reproduced the effect with statistics in prose, 41% against 20%, and removed it by adding a pictograph and a quiz, 38% against 44%. Winterbottom, Bekker, Conner and Mooney reviewed 17 studies. In five of them narrative information influenced decision making more than no extra information or statistical information did. First-person narratives were twice as likely as third-person ones to produce an effect. The honest summary is that the effect is real in the paradigm that names it and conditional everywhere else.

study.cite: Betsch, C., Haase, N., Renkewitz, F., & Schmid, P. (2015). The narrative bias revisited: What drives the biasing influence of narrative information on risk perceptions? Judgment and Decision Making, 10(3), 241-264.

limits: No effect size is carried in the structured fields, because the studies report standardised regression coefficients, percentages and chi-squares, and putting a β beside a percentage-point difference would suggest a comparison the papers do not support. The n recorded above is Experiment 2 alone; Experiment 1 had 277 subjects. Only Betsch and colleagues' 2015 paper was read in full, as the publisher's PDF at Cambridge, and its figures were extracted twice from the document text. The 2011, 2013, 2015 and 2020 papers by the same group were read only as their abstracts at Europe PMC, as were those by Ubel, Fagerlin, Obrecht and Winterbottom. The sample sizes and percentages quoted from them are the ones their authors chose to put in an abstract. Fagerlin's second study reports percentages this entry could not interpret with confidence, so its conclusion is given in words and its numbers are not. Five experiments in the core line come from one group at the University of Erfurt, and the sixth, Experiment 2 of the 2015 paper, is the same group on a United States online panel. Every study in that line uses a fictitious disease and a hypothetical vaccination, and the outcome is a stated intention rather than a vaccination. Borgida and Nisbett's 1977 study, named in the 2015 paper as the classic case, was not obtained, and the description of it here is that paper's. The search for tests of Taleb's narrative fallacy covered Crossref by title and by bibliographic query and Europe PMC by phrase. Crossref returns no empirical study of it by that name, and the 24 Europe PMC records for the phrase are commentary and editorials rather than studies of human subjects. Narrative transportation is a separate literature that this entry does not summarise: Braddock and Dillard's 2016 meta-analysis of narrative persuasion was not obtained, and no figure from it is quoted here. Allen and Preiss's 1997 meta-analysis comparing narrative and statistical evidence appeared only in a search-engine summary and was left out for that reason.
misreadings: The first error is to read Taleb's narrative fallacy and the tested narrative bias as one idea. Taleb's is a claim about explanation, that people cannot look at a sequence of facts without weaving a story into it, and chapter 6 offers no experiment of his own. The tested bias is a claim about weighting, that a sample of cases pulls a judgement away from a base rate presented in the same session. The second error is inherited from Taleb's own retelling of the study he leans on. He describes an experiment in which 'the subjects were forecasting professionals' who judged the odds of a massive flood in America against an earthquake in California causing a flood. In Tversky and Kahneman's paper the flood item went to 245 undergraduates at the University of British Columbia in April 1982. The wording is 'somewhere in North America in 1983'. The geometric means were 3.1% for the conjunction and 2.2% for the flood alone, p < .01. The forecasters were a separate group of 115 people at the Second International Congress on Forecasting in Istanbul in July 1982. They judged a different pair, about relations between the United States and the Soviet Union, at .47% against .14%. The third error is to take the bias as proof that stories beat numbers. Where the comparison is a narrative message against a statistical one, the largest meta-analysis of it finds the statistic ahead, at g = 0.066 across 32,321 participants, and the direction flips only when the issue is severe, personal or medical. The fourth is to treat the effect as a fixed property of people rather than of the display. It shows up on a visual analog scale asking how risky something feels. It largely vanishes on the same page when the question asks for a percentage. Fagerlin and colleagues switched it off by drawing the statistic as a pictograph. The last is to assume every paper titled 'narrative bias' is about the same thing. Moore and colleagues use the term for spin in the abstracts of clinical trials, which is a property of writing rather than of readers.
